steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper introducing MINT, a benchmark that evaluates LLMs in multi-turn interaction with tools and natural language feedback. Explain the motivation, describe the benchmark briefly, and summarize the main findings from our evaluation.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Motivation: multi-turn interaction, tools and feedback vs. current single-turn evaluation
- MINT: what it is and how it is built
- Evaluation setup and main results
- Further findings: feedback-providing ability, dataset artifacts, simulated vs human feedback
- Expected impact

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
To solve complex tasks, Large Language Models (LLMs) often need multiple rounds of interaction with the users, and sometimes external tools help them. How well LLMs perform over multiple turns of user-LLM exchanges is crucial in real-world applications: roughly 73% of Human-ChatGPT conversations have more than one turn, based on 94k entries of a conversation dataset. At the same time, being able to adapt to natural language feedback from users is also pivotal for how useful they are in practice. But current LLM evaluations mostly focus on single-turn input-output and often overlook natural language feedback provided by users, so there is a discrepancy between real-world use cases and evaluation. It is essential to measure how much LLMs can benefit from both tools and natural language feedback during multi-turn interaction, so that future research is incentivized to improve LLMs' capabilities in a broader range of real-world scenarios.

To bridge these gaps, we introduce MINT. MINT is a benchmark for LLMs that measures how they perform during multi-turn interaction, and it focuses on two capabilities in particular (§ 2.1): (1) tool-augmented task-solving; (2) leveraging natural language feedback. MINT mirrors the setting of real-world collaborative problem-solving between user, LLM and tool. To solve a problem, the LLM can use external tools by generating and executing Python programs and/or it can collect natural language feedback to refine its solutions. The feedback is provided by GPT-4, which is meant to simulate human users in a reproducible and scalable way. To make the evaluation comprehensive, we include eight established datasets that span reasoning, code generation, and decision-making (§ 2.2). We want multi-turn evaluation to be affordable, so after collecting 29,307 diverse instances from existing datasets (Tab. 1), we construct a subset of 586 challenging and representative instances which need multi-turn interaction to solve.

- Evaluation
  - 4 closed- and 16 open-source LLMs
  - tool use: performance from multi-turn tool use (§ 3.2); feedback: performance upon GPT-4 feedback (§ 3.3)
  - all models benefit: 1–8% per additional turn of tool use; 2–17% with feedback
  - better single-turn != better multi-turn: Claude-2 beats Claude-1 single-turn, but Claude-1 benefits more and is better with >2 turns
  - open vs closed gap: best open-source Lemur-70b-chat-v1 lags best closed-source by 8.7% absolute success rate (with feedback)
  - SIFT and RLHF hurt multi-turn performance on most LLMs, with or without feedback
    - SIFT: Codellama-34B by 11.1\% and 15.4\% (w/ feedback); RLHF: LLaMA-2-70B by 8.5\% and 8.7\%
    - exceptions: Vicuna-7B and Lemur-70b-chat-v1, where SIFT helps
- Further findings
  - fix evaluated LLM, change feedback-provider LLM -> measure feedback-providing ability (§ 3.4)
  - feedback-providing may be orthogonal to task-solving: CodeLLaMA-34B-Instruct worst at task-solving but improves GPT-3.5
  - undesired artifacts in the same conversation dataset, widely used for instruction tuning (§ 3.5)
  - GPT4-simulated feedback as helpful as human-written feedback, by human evaluation and task performance (§ 3.6)

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
To solve complex tasks, Large Language Models (LLMs) often need multiple rounds of interaction with the users, and sometimes external tools help them. How well LLMs perform over multiple turns of user-LLM exchanges is crucial in real-world applications: roughly 73% of Human-ChatGPT conversations have more than one turn, based on 94k entries of a conversation dataset. At the same time, being able to adapt to natural language feedback from users is also pivotal for how useful they are in practice. But current LLM evaluations mostly focus on single-turn input-output and often overlook natural language feedback provided by users, so there is a discrepancy between real-world use cases and evaluation. It is essential to measure how much LLMs can benefit from both tools and natural language feedback during multi-turn interaction, so that future research is incentivized to improve LLMs' capabilities in a broader range of real-world scenarios.

To bridge these gaps, we introduce MINT. MINT is a benchmark for LLMs that measures how they perform during multi-turn interaction, and it focuses on two capabilities in particular (§ 2.1): (1) tool-augmented task-solving; (2) leveraging natural language feedback. MINT mirrors the setting of real-world collaborative problem-solving between user, LLM and tool. To solve a problem, the LLM can use external tools by generating and executing Python programs and/or it can collect natural language feedback to refine its solutions. The feedback is provided by GPT-4, which is meant to simulate human users in a reproducible and scalable way. To make the evaluation comprehensive, we include eight established datasets that span reasoning, code generation, and decision-making (§ 2.2). We want multi-turn evaluation to be affordable, so after collecting 29,307 diverse instances from existing datasets (Tab. 1), we construct a subset of 586 challenging and representative instances which need multi-turn interaction to solve.

We evaluate 4 closed- and 16 open-source LLMs with MINT. To measure the tool-augmented task-solving capability of the LLMs, we analyze their performance from multi-turn tool use (§ 3.2). To assess how well they can leverage natural language feedback, we measure their performance upon natural language feedback by GPT-4 (§ 3.3). Our results show that:

- • All models benefit from tool interaction and natural language feedback. The absolute performance gains are 1–8% for each additional turn of tool use, and 2–17% with natural language feedback.

- • Better single-turn performance does not necessarily mean better multi-turn performance. For example, Claude-2 outperforms its predecessor Claude-1 in single-turn evaluation, but Claude-1 benefits more from interaction and performs better with >2 turns.

- • There is a notable gap between open- and closed-source LLMs in multi-turn interaction performance. For example, even with the help of language feedback, the best open-source model, Lemur-70b-chat-v1, lags behind the best closed-source model by 8.7% in absolute success rate.

- • On most of the LLMs we evaluated, models trained with supervised instruction fine-tuning (SIFT) and reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) perform worse in multi-turn settings, whether or not there is language feedback. For example, SIFT hurts the multi-turn performance of Codellama-34B by 11.1\% and 15.4\% (w/ feedback), and RLHF negatively affects LLaMA-2-70B by 8.5\% and 8.7\%, respectively. Vicuna-7B and Lemur-70b-chat-v1 are notable exceptions, where SIFT improves multi-turn interaction.

If we fix the LLM being evaluated and change the LLM that provides feedback, MINT can measure how well different LLMs provide useful feedback (§ 3.4). We find that the ability to provide feedback could be orthogonal to the ability to solve tasks: CodeLLaMA-34B-Instruct performs the worst in task-solving, but it can provide feedback that improves the stronger GPT-3.5. MINT's challenging evaluation also reveals undesired artifacts in that same conversation dataset, which is widely used for instruction tuning (§ 3.5). We also show that language feedback simulated by GPT4 is as helpful as feedback written by humans, based on human evaluation and task performance (§ 3.6).

We expect that MINT can help track progress and incentivize future research on improving LLMs' multi-turn task-solving and/or feedback-providing capabilities. This is especially true for open-source communities, where human evaluation can be less accessible than for commercial LLMs that have a large user base.
